slides.text:
Most languages let a function give back one value. A Go function can give back several at once, and the caller receives each of them. You will return pairs, ignore the ones you do not need, and use a second value to say whether the first one is usable.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
first, second = name(input)

name(input):
    give back a, b

slides.text: Instead of one type after the parentheses, the function lists a type for each value it returns, inside their own parentheses. `return` then lists as many values, in the same order.
The caller must receive every value. If it does not need one, it can drop it with `_`, the blank name that Go never asks you to use.

intro.title: A second value that says more

slides.text: A common use of two values: the first is the result, and the second is a `bool` that says whether the result can be trusted. The caller checks the flag before using the result. The snippet is pseudo code.
You can also **name** the returned values in the signature. They start as zero values inside the function, you assign them like variables, and a bare `return` gives them back.

slides.text: A function can return more than two values, of different types. And when a call returns several values, you can hand that whole call to another function as its arguments, with no variables in between. The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
outer(inner())

inner() gives back a, b
outer receives a and b

slides.text: Named results start at the zero value of their type, so you only assign them when the answer is not zero. A bare `return` can sit anywhere, even inside a loop, and gives back whatever the names hold at that moment.
